title: The living flame
hookLine: John's poem of love like a flame that wounds gently

cards: Same friar, a different voice. Yesterday John of the Cross was drawing a steep mountain with nothing written up its side. Today he's writing a love poem.

It opens with a cry, which in English runs something like this: O living flame of love, that tenderly wounds my soul in its deepest center. Wounds, and tenderly, in the same breath. That's not how burns usually go.
The man who taught letting go of everything also wrote lines this warm, and wrote them about God. For John, the two belong together.

teach.h: THE FLAME IS THE HOLY SPIRIT.
teach.b: John wrote the poem, and then, because a friend asked, a long commentary explaining it line by line. The flame, he says, is the Holy Spirit, an old image in the Bible.

At Pentecost, the book of Acts says, "there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." And the Song of Songs says love's coals "are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame."
So why would a loving flame wound? John uses a picture from the hearth.

teach.h: A DAMP LOG HISSES, THEN GLOWS.
teach.b: Put a damp log on a fire. At first the fire doesn't look friendly. The log hisses, blackens, smokes, and lets out the water it was holding.
That's the hard part, the purifying.

teach.h: ONE FIRE: THE HURT AND THE LOVE.
teach.b: But the fire is the same fire the whole time. It isn't angry at the log. It's turning the log into itself.
In the end the wood glows, and you can't tell where the log stops and the flame begins. For John, that's what God's love does to a person.
The pain of being changed and the joy of being loved are one fire, felt at different stages. So the wound is tender: love that hurts only because it's getting in.
And notice where the flame reaches: the deepest center, the same center Teresa put the King in, two days ago. The two friends seem to point at the same room. One built a castle around it.
The other set it on fire.

how: Carmelites and other readers of John of the Cross pray with his poems slowly, sometimes aloud, and his Living Flame of Love is read in retreats on the work of the Holy Spirit.

games.q: you're a damp log on John's fire. you hiss, you smoke, you blacken. what's happening, in his picture?
o: the same loving fire is turning you into itself.
games.why: John says the fire is one fire from start to finish. the hard part is the log letting go of its damp; the end is wood that glows.

practice: If you can do it safely, light a candle and just watch; if you can't, call a flame to mind, or look at a picture of one.
See how it moves, where it's blue and where it's gold, and how it turns whatever it touches into more of itself.
If you pray, let it stand for the Holy Spirit, as John did; if you don't, just watch the light, and blow out any real flame before the end.

wordCard.voice: The living flame. John of the Cross's image of the Holy Spirit's love: a fire that wounds gently, burns away what's damp, and turns the soul into flame.

carryVoice: Your line: o living flame. In John's poem, love reaches the deepest center. See you tomorrow.
